# Default Predicates and Filters of Auto-Generated Routes in Spring Cloud Gateway

When a microservices system has many services and constantly changing instance counts, declaring every route by hand can become tedious. In **SPRING_CLOUD_GATEWAY**, the **DiscoveryClient Route Definition Locator** can generate `RouteDefinition`s based on service names supplied by service discovery. The key is to understand: **which path will an auto-generated route accept, which service will it forward to, and which filters does it include by default?**

This lesson belongs to the **Service Discovery and Load Balancing** chapter, focusing on the default **Path Route Predicate** and **RewritePath GatewayFilter** of auto-generated routes. This is the foundation for combining route predicates, the filter chain, path/header transformations, service discovery, authentication, rate limiting, circuit breakers, retries, TLS, and request observability when building a secure API Gateway.

> **Scope:** The main configurations illustrate **Spring Cloud Gateway Server WebFlux** in lines using the `spring.cloud.gateway.discovery.locator.*` namespace, commonly seen in Gateway 4.x. In newer lines or **Gateway Server MVC**, starter names, namespaces, and features may differ. Verify the documentation for your exact Spring Boot, Spring Cloud release train, and Gateway versions before using.

## 1. Manual Routes vs. Auto-Generated Routes

A **manual route** lets you define the public API path, target service, and filters yourself:

~~~yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: inventory-api
          uri: lb://inventory-service
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/inventory/**
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=2
~~~

This configuration is chosen by the operator: the public URL is `/api/inventory/**`, and `StripPrefix=2` removes the two segments `api` and `inventory`. Using `uri: lb://inventory-service` **does not mean this is an auto-generated route**; the route is still completely manually declared.

An **auto-generated route** works differently: if the DiscoveryClient locator is enabled, the Gateway can retrieve the set of **service IDs** from `DiscoveryClient` or `ReactiveDiscoveryClient` and construct `RouteDefinition`s without needing static `routes` entries for each service.

~~~yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      discovery:
        locator:
          enabled: true
~~~

For example, if the registry returns service ID `inventory-service`, the Gateway can create a route for that service. Under the default mechanism, a client typically calls:

~~~http
GET /inventory-service/products/42?sort=price HTTP/1.1
Host: gateway.example.test
~~~

And downstream `inventory-service` receives path `/products/42`, preserving query `sort=price` unless other filters change it.

**Note:** setting `enabled: true` does not spin up a registry, register backends, or guarantee live instances exist. You still need a compatible discovery implementation, accurate service registration, and load balancing for `lb://`.

## 2. Default Components of an Auto-Generated Route

In general notation, the default predicate can be interpreted as **`Path=/{serviceId}/**`**: `{serviceId}` is replaced with the service ID when generating the route, rather than being a literal string clients must type.

For service ID `inventory-service`, the default model in Gateway Server WebFlux typically includes:

| Component | Default behavior | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **`Path` predicate** | Matches `/inventory-service/**` | Selects the route only when the path starts with the service name |
| **`RewritePath` filter** | Strips the leading `/inventory-service` segment from the path | Downstream receives the internal API path without the service ID prefix |
| **Target URI** | `lb://inventory-service` | Delegates instance selection to the load balancer |
| **Route ID** | Generated by the locator per implementation rules | Used for observing and managing routes; do not assume it equals the service ID verbatim |

Assuming a backend exposes `GET /products/42`:

~~~text
Client:
  GET /inventory-service/products/42?sort=price

Path predicate:
  /inventory-service/** -> match

RewritePath:
  /inventory-service/products/42 -> /products/42

URI:
  lb://inventory-service

Backend:
  GET /products/42?sort=price
~~~

Here **the predicate selects the route first**, the filter **rewrites the path afterward**, and then routing/load balancing chooses the target. The default `RewritePath` only handles the path prefix; it does not strip query strings, request headers, or JSON bodies.

### How are the default expressions interpreted?

When generating routes, the locator uses `serviceId` as a variable in configuration expressions. The two transformations can be expressed conceptually as:

~~~text
Path predicate:
  / + serviceId + /**

RewritePath:
  regexp      = / + serviceId + /?(?<remaining>.*)
  replacement = /${remaining}

Destination:
  lb://serviceId
~~~

`remaining` is a regex capture group: the portion of the path remaining after the service ID prefix. This is an **illustrative formula to explain behavior**, not YAML for a static route. When customizing the DiscoveryClient locator, dynamic config expressions and regex replacement group escaping must follow your running version.

**Do not confuse static routes with auto-generated routes**: in a static route, `/inventory-service/**` is a fixed literal value; in the auto-generating locator, the corresponding value is produced for **each service ID**.

~~~mermaid
flowchart TD
    REG["Registry: inventory-service"] --> DISC["DiscoveryClient"]
    DISC --> LOC["DiscoveryClientRouteDefinitionLocator"]
    LOC --> DEF["RouteDefinition: Path, RewritePath, lb://"]
    DEF --> ROUTE["RouteLocator: Executable route"]
    REQ["GET /inventory-service/products/42"] --> MATCH{"Does Path match?"}
    ROUTE --> MATCH
    MATCH -->|No| OTHER["Check other routes"]
    MATCH -->|Yes| REWRITE["RewritePath -> /products/42"]
    REWRITE --> LB["Load balancer selects instance"]
    LB --> DOWN["Backend inventory-service"]
    DOWN --> RESP["Response to client"]
~~~

## 3. DiscoveryClient and LoadBalancer Have Different Responsibilities

Many errors are lumped under "discovery" even though they happen at different stages.

**Service discovery** answers: *Which service IDs and instances are registered?* **DiscoveryClient Route Definition Locator** answers: *Should a route be created for that service ID, and what are its request-matching rules?* **Spring Cloud LoadBalancer** answers: *Among available instances of the service, which instance does this request go to?*

Suppose the registry supplies:

~~~text
inventory-service
  - instance A: 10.20.1.11:8080
  - instance B: 10.20.1.12:8080

billing-service
  - instance C: 10.20.2.21:8080
~~~

The locator can generate **one route for inventory-service** and **one route for billing-service**, without needing separate routes for instances A and B. When a request matches the inventory route, the load balancer selects A or B.

| System change | Does the auto-generated route need to change? | Can instance selection change? |
|---|---|---|
| Add a new service ID | May need to refresh/create a new route | Yes |
| Add an instance for an existing service | Not necessarily | Yes |
| One instance disconnects | Route may still exist | Yes |
| Change locator `Path`/`RewritePath` | Must apply config and refresh routes | Not directly |
| A service has zero instances left | Route may still remain | Cannot pick an available instance |

Actual behavior also depends on caching and the DiscoveryClient/LoadBalancer refresh mechanism. **Having a route does not prove a healthy backend exists**; a request can match a path yet fail because the load balancer finds no instance.

## 4. Prerequisites for Auto-Generated Routes to Work

A Gateway environment needs at minimum:

1. **Gateway Server WebFlux** matching your web stack and release train.
2. A **`DiscoveryClient` or `ReactiveDiscoveryClient`** matching your chosen registry, such as Eureka, Consul, or orchestration-platform integration.
3. A registry with **real service IDs** and properly registered backend instances.
4. The **discovery locator enabled** property under the exact namespace for your version.
5. A **load balancing** mechanism to handle `lb://` URIs; typically Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, such as `spring-cloud-starter-loadbalancer` if not already present.
6. Network connectivity from the Gateway to backend instances, including DNS/service discovery, TLS, and appropriate firewalls.

Example configuration on the **Gateway locator side**:

~~~yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: edge-gateway
  cloud:
    gateway:
      discovery:
        locator:
          enabled: true
          lower-case-service-id: true
~~~

This is **not a complete Eureka/Consul/Kubernetes configuration**; each solution needs its own starter and properties. `lower-case-service-id: true` is helpful when a registry, such as some Eureka setups, returns uppercase service names while operators want lowercase URL paths.

However, do not assume every registry handles casing or normalizes service IDs identically: check the **raw name from `DiscoveryClient`**, the **actual generated `Path`**, and the **final `lb://...` URI**.

## 5. Default Path and RewritePath: What to Verify Directly

When a service is named `orders`, for example:

~~~text
GET /orders/api/v1/42
~~~

By default, the Route Predicate matches `/orders/**` and the rewrite filter strips `/orders` so the backend can receive:

~~~text
GET /api/v1/42
~~~

This solves a common mismatch: **the backend does not need to know the Gateway's service ID prefix**.

Three scenarios should be distinguished:

| Scenario | Typical outcome | Diagnosis |
|---|---|---|
| No route matches `/orders/**` | 404 if no other handler matches | Check locator, service ID, Path/casing, and route order |
| Route matches, wrong rewrite leaves backend receiving `/orders/api/v1/42` | Backend may return 404 | Check RewritePath and actual path received by backend |
| Route matches, rewrite works, but no instances exist | Instance-selection/routing error, typically 5xx or 404 per config | Check registry instances, LoadBalancer, and connectivity |

**Do not infer from HTTP status alone.** It is best to use backend echo/logging to see the received path and enable controlled observability for route ID, request URI, and selected instance.

### The default is not a mandatory public URL rule

Many products want URLs like `/api/orders/**` instead of `/orders/**`. In that case you can:

- Write **manual routes** with a clear public prefix and appropriate `StripPrefix`/`RewritePath`.
- Customize the DiscoveryClient locator's predicate/filter templates for your version.
- Generate routes through a reviewed/approved configuration pipeline independent of internal service IDs.

When using the locator while wanting an `/api/{serviceId}/**` prefix, **you must update both Path and RewritePath in sync**. Changing only Path leaves downstream receiving the wrong path; changing only RewritePath can prevent the route from ever matching the new public URL.

## 6. Customizing the Predicates List: Easy to Lose the Default Path

This is the most error-prone spot in this topic: **when overriding `discovery.locator.predicates`, do not assume the Gateway still adds the original Path automatically**.

The Gateway documentation advises: if you want custom predicates **while keeping default behavior**, you must **re-declare the default Path** alongside the new predicates.

### Example: adding Method

Suppose an auto-generated route should only accept GET along with the service-ID-prefixed Path:

~~~yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      discovery:
        locator:
          enabled: true
          predicates:
            - name: Path
              args:
                pattern: "'/' + serviceId + '/**'"
            - name: Method
              args:
                methods: "'GET'"
~~~

This example shows the locator declaration structure using **expressions based on `serviceId`**. Exact field names, bound value types, and `Method` expression syntax must be verified against your exact Gateway version; the main point here is **keeping Path** when adding a new condition.

Logically, predicates on the same route combine with **AND**. Thus a `POST /orders/42` request does not match a route allowing only GET, even though the Path matches.

If you accidentally leave only the `Method` predicate without Path, the route can become **far too broad**, overlapping other routes and routing requests to unintended backends. This is especially dangerous when the locator is enabled across many internal services.

### Defaults do not automatically protect access

Even with a valid Path, the Gateway does not automatically distinguish public from internal service IDs. If the registry contains `internal-admin`, `/internal-admin/**` can become an unintended entry point if the locator is enabled without restrictions. You must **filter the service ID list**, apply network segmentation, and enforce authentication/authorization.

## 7. Customizing the Filters List: Easy to Lose the Default RewritePath

Similarly, when you set `discovery.locator.filters` to add a custom filter, **you must verify whether the default RewritePath is preserved**.

For example, suppose every request to an auto-generated service should include a diagnostic header `X-Edge-Discovery: gateway`. The intended filter pipeline is:

~~~text
1. RewritePath:
     regexp      = '/' + serviceId + '/?(?<remaining>.*)'
     replacement = '/${remaining}'

2. AddRequestHeader:
     name  = X-Edge-Discovery
     value = gateway
~~~

If you declare only the `AddRequestHeader` filter without `RewritePath`, the backend may receive the service ID prefix too. Requests to `/orders/api/v1/42` still match Path but get forwarded with an unintended path.

### Property-style reference example

Discovery locator configuration often expresses factory names and `args` as property paths, where certain arguments are **SpEL expressions** evaluated per service ID:

~~~properties
spring.cloud.gateway.discovery.locator.enabled=true
spring.cloud.gateway.discovery.locator.filters[0].name=RewritePath
spring.cloud.gateway.discovery.locator.filters[0].args[regexp]='/' + serviceId + '/?(?<remaining>.*)'
spring.cloud.gateway.discovery.locator.filters[0].args[replacement]="'/${remaining}'"
spring.cloud.gateway.discovery.locator.filters[1].name=AddRequestHeader
spring.cloud.gateway.discovery.locator.filters[1].args[name]=X-Edge-Discovery
spring.cloud.gateway.discovery.locator.filters[1].args[value]=gateway
~~~

**Note:** `args[replacement]` in this example is a **SpEL string literal** representing the replacement path using the `remaining` regex group. When converting between `.properties` and YAML, check how your running version interprets `${remaining}` (property placeholder vs. regex replacement) and escaping rules. Compare with the sample expression in the *DiscoveryClient Route Definition Locator* guide for your version, then verify the actual path with an integration test.

`AddRequestHeader` operates on request headers, while `RewritePath` operates on the request path. The two filters serve separate goals; a header filter **cannot replace** stripping the path prefix.

### Locator syntax is not the same as static routes

A typical static route looks like:

~~~yaml
predicates:
  - Path=/orders/**
filters:
  - StripPrefix=1
~~~

Here the name `orders` is **hardcoded**. The discovery locator needs expressions parameterized by `serviceId` to generate routes for many services; you cannot copy a filter block written for one fixed service name and assume it works for all services.

## 8. Extending Public Prefixes and Backend Paths

Suppose the team wants the public URL:

~~~text
/api/inventory-service/products/42
~~~

while the inventory backend expects:

~~~text
/products/42
~~~

A custom locator configuration must express:

| Stage | Desired rule |
|---|---|
| Route matching | `Path=/api/{serviceId}/**` |
| Rewrite | Strip the entire `/api/{serviceId}` prefix |
| Routing | Pick backend using URI `lb://{serviceId}` |

Do not just add `/api` to Path while leaving the default RewritePath that strips only `/{serviceId}`, because the leading `/api` prevents the regex from matching the start of the path. The backend would then receive `/api/inventory-service/products/42` verbatim and return 404.

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Client /api/inventory-service/products/42"] --> B["Path matches /api/inventory-service/**"]
    B --> C["RewritePath strips /api/inventory-service"]
    C --> D["/products/42"]
    D --> E["lb://inventory-service"]
    E --> F["Backend instance"]
~~~

**Design consideration:** In public APIs, URLs are part of the client contract. Service IDs are implementation details that may change when services are split or merged. Often, manual routes with stable public URLs are a better fit than exposing raw registry service names.

## 9. Controlling Which Services Get Auto-Generated Routes

A registry might contain:

~~~text
catalog
orders
billing
internal-admin
metrics-agent
~~~

If the locator is enabled on a public Gateway without restricting service IDs, the system risks generating `/internal-admin/**` or `/metrics-agent/**` routes as well, depending on what `DiscoveryClient` sees. That is why auto-generated routes need **an allowlist and network access policy**.

Some Gateway versions support `include-expression`, using a SpEL expression to decide whether to generate a route for a service ID. Illustrative example:

~~~yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      discovery:
        locator:
          enabled: true
          include-expression: "serviceId == 'catalog' or serviceId == 'orders'"
~~~

This expression works only if the registry literally returns `catalog` and `orders` with that casing. If the registry provides `CATALOG`, the case-sensitive comparison must be adjusted and verified. **Do not enable `lower-case-service-id` and assume the filter expression automatically runs on the lowercase ID**; observe the actual `DiscoveryClient` data and generated routes in your exact version.

In real systems, you also need:

- Scoping service discovery by environment/namespace to avoid mixing public and internal services uncontrollably.
- Spring Security or equivalent authentication/authorization at the right layer.
- NetworkPolicy, firewalls, and preventing external clients from bypassing directly to backends.
- Per-API rate limiting rather than keying solely on client-supplied headers.
- Protection for route and discovery management endpoints; never let the Internet mutate routes dynamically.

## 10. Global Filters and Auto-Generated Route Filters

After a `RouteDefinition` is generated and turned into a `Route`, requests still flow through the Gateway filter chain.

| Type | Typical scope | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Discovery locator filters** | Filter template used to build auto-generated routes | Default RewritePath, adding headers to discovery routes |
| **`default-filters`** | Filters attached to routes by Gateway's default mechanism | Shared `SetRequestHeader` |
| **`GlobalFilter`** | Gateway pipeline after a Route is selected | Trace/correlation ID, cross-cutting policies |
| **`WebFilter`** | Spring WebFlux pipeline before/around route matching | Spring Security, blocking requests at the web tier |
| **Load-balancing routing filter** | Resolves `lb://` URI schemes in the Gateway chain | Selecting a service instance |

These groups are **not synonymous**. Adding a `default-filter` does not mean you edited `discovery.locator.filters`; and a `GlobalFilter` does not mean unmatched requests pass through it.

Execution order depends on `Ordered`, route filters, and internal filters. When multiple filters modify the same path or headers, verify the **actual request arriving at the backend** rather than guessing solely from YAML line order.

### Relationship with retries, circuit breakers, and TLS

An auto-generated route can integrate `Retry` or `CircuitBreaker` depending on version, but those mechanisms **do not appear automatically just by enabling DiscoveryClient**. Control timeouts, backoff, retry counts, and idempotency—especially for write requests.

Similarly, an `lb://serviceId` URI only indicates load-balanced target resolution; to protect traffic in transit, configure TLS for client → Gateway and Gateway → downstream according to policy. Never assume every `lb://` URI automatically uses HTTPS or validates certificates.

## 11. Step-by-Step Troubleshooting

An effective approach is to isolate whether the failure lies in **route generation**, **route matching**, **path rewriting**, or **instance selection**.

| Symptom | Suspected stage | Evidence to check |
|---|---|---|
| No routes auto-generated | DiscoveryClient / locator | `enabled` under right namespace, registry has service IDs, refreshed yet |
| Route exists, but `/orders/**` returns 404 at Gateway | Path matching | Exact service ID casing, runtime Route predicate, route order |
| Backend receives `/orders/items` instead of `/items` | RewritePath | Whether locator filters preserved RewritePath, regex/replacement accuracy |
| Route matches, but no backend reached | LoadBalancer / discovery instances | Instance list, health/status registration, load balancer dependency |
| Intermittent success and 5xx | Some backend instances failing or connection/TLS issue | Selected instance, logs, health checks |
| After customizing Method, GET hits wrong backend | Lost Path predicate, route matches too broadly | New predicate list and route order |
| After adding a header filter, backend returns 404 | Lost default RewritePath | Compare downstream path before and after |
| Registry added a service, Gateway doesn't see it yet | Cache / refresh | Current service IDs and runtime Routes on each node |
| Internal service route exposed publicly | Allowlist / registry scope | `include-expression`, network boundaries, route security |
| Uppercase service ID causes mismatch | Case normalization | Registry ID, generated Path, `lb://` URI |

### Which observability tools should you use?

1. Check **runtime dependencies and startup logs**: Gateway Server WebFlux, discovery implementation, and load balancer.
2. Check **actual service IDs and instances** from `DiscoveryClient`.
3. Inspect **generated routes**: ID, URI, Path predicate, RewritePath, and order.
4. Send requests through the Gateway and compare the **client path** with the **backend path**.
5. Observe route ID, status, latency, retries, and target instance via logging/metrics/tracing when configured.

Some Spring Cloud Gateway versions provide Actuator Gateway endpoints for routes/refresh. Expose management endpoints only when truly needed, protect them with authentication/network rules, and consult version-specific docs. In multi-node Gateway deployments, refreshing one node does not necessarily synchronize every node.

## 12. Hands-On: Verifying Default Path and RewritePath

**Test conditions:**

- Gateway Server WebFlux running on port `8080`.
- `DiscoveryClient` connected to a registry with service ID `inventory-service` registered.
- An inventory instance serving `GET /products/42` that can echo/log the raw path.
- LoadBalancer for `lb://` active and the discovery locator enabled for your version.

### Step 1 — Inspect the runtime Route

Before sending HTTP traffic, confirm the Gateway generated a route for service ID `inventory-service`. Record its URI (`lb://inventory-service` or registry representation), actual Path predicate, and actual RewritePath. **Do not guess the route ID; record the actual generated ID.**

### Step 2 — Send a valid request

~~~bash
curl -i "http://localhost:8080/inventory-service/products/42?sort=price"
~~~

The backend should receive path `/products/42` and query `sort=price`, assuming no other filters intervene. The HTTP response depends on the backend endpoint.

### Step 3 — Send URLs outside the default Path

~~~bash
curl -i "http://localhost:8080/products/42"
curl -i "http://localhost:8080/unknown-service/products/42"
~~~

These requests do not match the default `inventory-service` route. Without another matching route/handler, they typically return 404. This **does not prove `DiscoveryClient` is broken**; it shows those URLs do not match the pattern generated for that service.

### Step 4 — Test missing service instances

In the lab, deregister the inventory instances or stop the backend. If the route still exists while LoadBalancer cannot pick an instance, the Gateway usually returns an error like **503** (or another code per config), rather than a route-miss 404. Distinguish "no route," "no instance," and "instance returned an error."

### Step 5 — Customize filters and observe

In a test environment, replace the locator filters config with **only a header-adding filter**, omitting RewritePath. Refresh routes properly, call the default URL again, and observe that the backend may receive `/inventory-service/products/42`. Then restore your version's default RewritePath and verify the backend receives `/products/42`.

| Test | Client path | Expected backend path | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Default locator | `/inventory-service/products/42` | `/products/42` | Path + RewritePath working |
| Locator missing RewritePath | `/inventory-service/products/42` | May still include service ID | Default was replaced |
| Wrong Path | `/products/42` | Not forwarded on this route | Predicate did not match |
| Route exists, no instances | `/inventory-service/products/42` | No instance receives it | Load-balancing failure, not Path |

### Step 6 — Record test evidence

Save the **service ID, route ID, URI, loaded predicates/filters, path received by backend, selected instance, and response code**. Never record raw tokens, session cookies, or queries containing personal data. For multi-environment APIs, also test uppercase service IDs, URIs with query parameters, backend 404s, and service scale-up/scale-down events.

## 13. Auto-Generated Routes vs. Manual Routes?

| Criterion | Auto-generated routes | Manual routes |
|---|---|---|
| Many services with uniform URL conventions | Less repetitive config | Requires adding routes/config files |
| Services appear/disappear dynamically | Fits well when discovery/caching is well managed | Usually requires a route-update workflow |
| Public URLs must stay stable despite internal renames | Requires careful customization | Easy to decouple external URLs from service IDs |
| Different security policies per API | Needs detailed allowlists/policies | Easier per-route review, though security is still required |
| Concern about exposing internal services | Must tightly control registry scope and `include-expression` | Can declare only approved APIs |
| Need load balancing across instances | Uses `lb://` | Also supports `lb://` without auto-routes |

**Practical recommendation:** use auto-generated routes when the registry/namespace is tightly controlled, all included services are approved for exposure, and service-ID URL prefixes fit. Use manual routes or an approved configuration pipeline when APIs have public contracts and distinct authorization requirements. In both cases, `lb://` still gives you load balancing.

## 14. Pre-Deployment Checklist

- [ ] I have verified the Gateway version, Spring Cloud version, and exact WebFlux/MVC web stack.
- [ ] `DiscoveryClient` is active and returns the expected service IDs.
- [ ] LoadBalancer or an equivalent mechanism is present to resolve `lb://` URIs.
- [ ] I understand the default Path predicate typically matches `/{serviceId}/**`.
- [ ] I understand the default RewritePath filter strips the `/{serviceId}` prefix before forwarding.
- [ ] I have verified that queries/headers/bodies are not unintentionally altered by path rewriting.
- [ ] When customizing the predicates list, I **preserve Path** if default matching is still needed.
- [ ] When customizing the filters list, I **preserve RewritePath** if default prefix stripping is still needed.
- [ ] I have checked `serviceId`-based expressions and regex replacement escaping for my version.
- [ ] I have handled service ID casing and cross-checked the actual Path and `lb://` URI.
- [ ] I do not automatically expose internal services through a public registry.
- [ ] I have separately configured authentication, authorization, rate limiting, retries/circuit breakers, and TLS.
- [ ] I have tested three separate errors: no route match, wrong downstream path, and no instance selected.
- [ ] I have verified route refresh/caching and the state of all Gateway nodes when the registry changes.
- [ ] I expose management endpoints only with appropriate access controls.

- [Spring Cloud Gateway Reference](https://docs.spring.io/spring-cloud-gateway/reference/) — **DiscoveryClient Route Definition Locator**, default predicates/filters, and version-specific customization.
- [Spring Cloud Gateway Project](https://spring.io/projects/spring-cloud-gateway) — project information and release trains.
- [Spring Cloud Commons — Common Abstractions](https://docs.spring.io/spring-cloud-commons/reference/spring-cloud-commons/common-abstractions.html) — DiscoveryClient and Spring Cloud LoadBalancer.

- [Spring Boot Actuator](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/actuator/) — endpoint management and security principles.

**Remember:** In auto-generated routes, **the default Path uses the service ID prefix** to match requests and **the default RewritePath strips that prefix** before calling downstream. **Overriding the discovery locator's predicates/filters lists can drop default behavior**, so explicitly re-declare required components, test the actual path received, and strictly control which services are allowed through the Gateway.
